Passenger demand overhaul: recalibrated against real traffic, and markets that grow with service (new games)

October 29, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

We checked the game’s passenger demand against real ticket data: every US city pair in the US Department of Transportation’s airfare survey and every Australian domestic route in the government’s route statistics. The big routes were close, but the game had about four times as many US domestic passengers as the real world, almost all of them in small cities and short hops. Australia had only about half its real traffic. New games now use a recalibrated model:

  • Short trips are driven, not flown. In the US and Australia, demand now fades on routes under about 650 km, the way it does when most people take the car. Orlando to Miami no longer looks like New York to Los Angeles.
  • Small towns lose travellers to big airports nearby. If a much bigger airport is within a few hours’ drive, many locals use it, so a small US airport next to a major hub has a smaller market of its own.
  • US city size matters more. Small US cities generate fewer trips per person than the old model gave them, so regional routes are thinner, and the right aircraft for them is smaller.
  • Theme-park and casino cities are sized more realistically. Most visitors to places like Orlando and Las Vegas arrive by car, so they count for less air demand than visitors to island resorts like Hawaii.
  • Australia flies more. Long domestic routes such as Sydney–Melbourne, Brisbane–Cairns and Perth to the mining towns get substantially more demand. Short hops within New South Wales get less.
  • Seasons follow real traffic. Every US and Australian airport now has its own seasonal pattern, taken from three years of real passenger numbers. Florida and Arizona are busiest in winter, Seattle, Boston and Chicago in summer. Ski towns like Vail and Aspen do most of their year between December and March, and Darwin and Cairns peak in the dry season.
  • Regions fly differently. Westerners fly far more than the old model gave them credit for, and the Northeast and Midwest fly a little less. On top of that, each US and Australian airport is matched to its real traffic, and airports we have no data for take their region’s figure.
  • Busy short-haul corridors. Short hops are now judged on real driving times rather than distance, so a mountain pass counts for what it is. California, the Pacific Northwest and the Texas Triangle fly far more short-haul than other regions. The New York–Philadelphia–Washington corridor loses travellers to the train, and Floridians drive. Mountain resorts like Aspen, Jackson Hole and Sun Valley keep their short flights, because nobody drives the pass if they can fly it.
  • Double-counted cities fixed. A few secondary airports were carrying their whole metro’s population a second time: St. Petersburg (Tampa), Sanford (Orlando), Mesa (Phoenix), Newport News (Norfolk), Everett (Seattle) and a few smaller ones. Each now has its own share of the city instead.

We deliberately stopped short of full realism, about two-thirds of the way there, so regional flying stays playable. Routes outside the US and Australia are unchanged until we have real data to check them against.

Markets also stop being fixed. Until now every city pair had a set size, whoever flew it and however often. In new games a market now grows with the service it gets, and fades when that service leaves:

  • New routes build their market. A city pair nobody flies starts at 70% of its full size. Fly it and the market grows over the following year, which replaces the old 16-week ramp-up. About twice a day at the going fare brings it to full size (daily gets it to about 90%), and more flights or lower fares grow it further, up to 30% above normal.
  • Markets remember. Cut a route and its market fades over months, not overnight. A rival who moves in soon after takes over most of what you built, and so can you after a rival leaves.
  • Everyone builds the same market. Your flights and your rivals’ all count toward the size of a market, but your frequency, brand and product still decide who carries the passengers. A newcomer on a busy route now wins its share gradually instead of shrinking the whole market.
  • The world starts settled. Routes the rival airlines already fly start at their full size, so a new game opens on real-world demand rather than in a slump.

Both changes are switched on by default for new games, and you can turn market development off on the setup screen. Games already in progress keep the demand they started with. More on how demand works in the route economics guide.
